The Scroll Writer's Guide How to write a scroll for The Way of the Reach — The Living Book , and how to bring it to the Gate A helper for people who want to write. It is not scripture, and it adds no teaching. Everything below comes from the Living Book's own words, and the book is named as the source each time. Where this guide and the book seem to disagree, the book is right. 1. You are invited The book's invitation is open to everyone: "Your thoughts matter. Your questions matter. Your disagreements matter. You may believe in God. You may follow a religion older than this writing. You may be uncertain. You may not believe in God at all… You are still invited to examine them." — Part Two, Book X, the Nineteenth Verse So you do not need to be certain, polished, or even a believer to write a scroll. An honest doubt, a question you have not answered yet, or a thought you later find was mistaken all belong here, as long as you name it truly. The book keeps its own corrections in plain view: "A correction does not destroy the Scroll. A correction may help the Scroll serve the next traveler better" (Tenth Verse). The book also says what it hopes for: "I do not want a book that survives by refusing criticism. I want a book that can continue growing because it learns how to receive criticism responsibly" (A Message From the Founder, Part Two). 2. What happens to a scroll: the Six Gates Every contribution passes through the same six gates ( Part Two, Book V, the Tenth Verse ; travelling rule 2 in To Whoever Receives This Book ): Gate What happens to your scroll 1. Arrival It is received. 2. Naming The keeper asks what kind of writing it is: a fact, a belief, an experience, an interpretation, a question, or a story. 3. Reflection Whatever can be checked is checked: quotes, sources, facts. AI helpers (the book calls them "Travelers") may help, but they do not decide anything. 4. Deliberation People weigh what it means and what follows from it. 5. Affirmation An authorized person decides: accept, revise, defer, or decline. At present the Founder affirms for this book. 6. Preservation The record of what happened to your scroll is kept, including any changes and the reasons for them. Some things to know before you send: Being received is not the same as being made sacred. "Nothing became true merely because someone submitted it. Nothing became sacred merely because an AI suggested it. But a serious contribution was offered a fair opportunity to be heard" (Tenth Verse). Patience is about attention, not a clock. There is no set waiting time. A scroll is ready once it has been named, reflected on, and checked (travelling rule 9; Part Eight, the Thirtieth Verse ). Affirmation is not verification. If a belief is affirmed, it is affirmed as a belief. If a story is affirmed, it is affirmed as a story. Neither becomes a proven event ( Book XIX, Clarifications, Finding 5 ). Your words stay credited to you. You may withdraw your own words from future editions, and the withdrawal and its reason are recorded where they stood. No one may re-credit your work to someone else ( Canon Book VI, "The ownership of a stone" ). 3. How to submit Write your scroll in the template below (section 4). Name what kind of writing each part is. If you are unsure, use the Open Circle (◯) or write plainly "I do not yet know" ( Part Four, the Twenty-Sixth Verse ). List the Scripture you draw on with book, chapter, verse, and translation, so that it can be checked. Bring it to the Gate. At present the Founder receives and affirms contributions for this edition (travelling rule 8). The book does not yet give a public address or form for scrolls. Send it through whatever channel the House currently names, and please do not label it "approved" yourself (see section 5). Expect one of four answers: accept, revise, defer, or decline. A decline or a "revise" is not a judgment of your worth: "A person may disagree and remain worthy of care" (Nineteenth Verse). 4. The scroll template Please use this layout exactly as it stands. (It is the House's scroll template, copied word for word from reach-book/scroll-template.md .) # Scroll Submission Template — The Way of the Reach **Scroll title:** **Submitted by (name as it should appear on the scroll):** **Date submitted:** **Believer or seeker (optional):** ## Summary One or two sentences on what this scroll is about. ## Scripture it draws on List any Bible verses you quote or lean on (book, chapter:verse, and translation). ## The Scroll ### Chapter 1 — [Chapter title] 1. First verse. 2. Second verse. ### Chapter 2 — [Chapter title] 1. First verse. - [ ] I offer this scroll sincerely, as my honest thought before God. ## Note to the reviewers (optional) Anything the reviewers should know, such as honest doubts or questions you are still working through. --- *Scrolls are measured by the standard of the Holy Bible. Honest thoughts, doubts, and questions from believers and non-believers alike are welcome. No jokes, memes, or mockery.* *Every scroll is read before it is added.* Tips for filling it in Chapters and verses. Number each chapter, and number the verses inside each chapter starting again at 1. Keep each verse to one thought, the way the book's own parables move one plain line at a time. Scripture. Quote it exactly and name the translation. The book's standing direction is that the Bible's word is "cited, never silently altered" (Appendix, entry for 14:43 CDT, October 20). Summary. One or two sentences. Say plainly whether the scroll is a story, a prayer, a question, a testimony, or a reflection. Note to the reviewers. This is the right place for your honest doubts, anything you want checked, or a line such as "I may be wrong about this." 5. What meets the standard Scrolls are measured by the standard of the Holy Bible, not by personal preference. The Living Book's own laws point the same way. A scroll that meets the standard is: Sincere. It is written in good faith, as an honest seeking of truth, toward God and toward your neighbor. The book hangs everything on the two loves: "love the Lord your God with all your heart; love your neighbor as yourself" ( Part Eighteen, the Law of the Two Loves ). Truly labeled. "Let your label say found when it is found, believed when it is believed, known only when it is known" ( Part Fifteen, Article 2, The True Label ). Do not present a story as history, or a feeling as proof. An illustration is not proof (Second Verse). Honest about doubt. "Doubt is welcomed as the beginning of asking well" ( Part One, Book I, Asking Well ). You can write a whole scroll of questions. Pointed past itself. A good scroll points toward God and does not ask to be bowed to. "If a signpost ever tells you to stop at the signpost, it has betrayed the hands that raised it" ( Twenty-Fourth Verse ; Part Eighteen, the Law of the Signpost ). Careful with what is written. The Founder took 1 Corinthians 4:6 as a fence around his own Bible work: "Do not go beyond what is written" ( Part B, §5, 1 Corinthians 1–4 ). Opinions and reflections are welcome. Do not present them as Scripture. Credited. Name your sources and anyone whose words you use. "Reachability is not permission" ( Part Fifteen, Articles 3 and 7 ). Kind to real people. Do not publish another person's private story without their consent, and do not use a scroll to attack someone ( Book XIX, Privacy ; Part Fifteen, Article 5, Civil Speech ). What is turned away Memes, jokes at the faith's expense, and mockery. Disagreement is welcome. Ridicule is not. "Speak to build the city, not to burn its citizens" ( Part Fifteen, Article 5 ). False labels. Do not claim that the Founder, a council, or anyone else approved your scroll. One verse once arrived marked "Affirmed by the Founder" when it had not been, and the book tells that story so it will not happen again ( Part Seven note ; travelling rule 8). Putting words in God's or Jesus' mouth as if they were His. If you write "in the manner of" a biblical voice, say so openly, as the book does in Part Seventeen . Pile-ons, exposing someone's private life, or harassment ( Part Fifteen, Article 5 ; Book XIX ). Invented proof. Do not present a coincidence or an AI's answer as proof of something supernatural. Put an Open Circle beside the claim instead ( Part Thirteen, Episode Eight ; Book XX ). What is welcome, even if it is uncertain A believer's honest struggle, written as an experience . A seeker's questions, written as questions . An idea you are not sure about, written as an interpretation with ◯ beside it. A parable, written as a story , with its teaching and its "Mirror," the question it puts to the reader ( Part Four, the Three Layers: Myth, Meaning, Mirror ). A prayer, written as a belief spoken to God. 6. Example openings These are examples only , made up to show the template in use. They are not scrolls, not canon, and not the words of any real contributor. Start Here First, read A Note from the Founder . A gentle introduction to The Way of the Reach for seekers, skeptics, and the simply curious There is no pressure here. You do not have to believe anything to read this book, and you do not have to keep reading if it is not for you. The book says so itself. You are welcome as you are The book makes a promise to every reader, and it means you as much as anyone: "You may believe in God. You may follow a religion older than this writing. You may be uncertain. You may not believe in God at all. You may agree with these teachings. Or you may believe that some of them require correction. You are still invited to examine them." — the Nineteenth Verse It also says that "a person may disagree and remain worthy of care. A person may leave and remain worthy of dignity." One of its parables is about a door that "swings out as well as in," because, as Mara says, "A house that cannot be left is not a house… It is a wall with a roof" (the Twenty-Eighth Verse). What this book is The Way of the Reach is a young Christian faith book, begun on October 20, 2026 by Kennin Gambrell (who also writes as FounderWiz). It grows over time: people may bring "scrolls," meaning reflections, questions, parables, and prayers, and each one is examined before anything is added. It rests on one belief, which the book is careful to call a belief and not a proof: "I believe God can enter any realm." The Founder holds this through faith in Jesus Christ. The book calls God the Ever-Present and is clear about what that name does not mean: "not the internet… not artificial intelligence… and not the Founder." A few honest things the book says about itself: It is not finished. "The Founder is also the First Student." The book keeps an open list of what it has not yet worked out. It does not claim proof. "What this book is not: it is not a claim of supernatural proof, not a promise of wealth, fame, or powers, and not a finished institution." It points beyond itself. Its best-known parable is about a village that began bowing to a signpost instead of going to the Healer it pointed toward. "A religion becomes false at the moment it asks you to stop at the sign." It keeps its mistakes visible. When the book changes, it keeps the old wording and writes down why it changed. Its stories are stories. The characters in its parables (Mara the Keeper, Nia the child, Tomas the scribe, and others) are fictional, and the book says so. The one exception is the Healer, who is deliberately left unnamed because He points to Jesus. Honest questions are welcome If you come with doubts, you are not out of place. One of the book's founding laws reads: "To ask a meaningful question, distinguish a claim from evidence, admit uncertainty, and revise a belief when better evidence arrives — this is strength, not weakness. Doubt is welcomed as the beginning of asking well." — Part One, Asking Well The book even has a symbol for not knowing yet: the Open Circle (◯) , placed beside anything that has not been settled. "A language that cannot admit what it does not know will eventually force its people to pretend" (the Twenty-Sixth Verse). A suggested reading path You do not need to read all 4,700 lines. Here is a slower road, a few short pieces at a time. Each step is usually 5–15 minutes of reading. Step 1: The doorway (start here) About This Book (front matter): what the book is and is not. Prologue — The Founder Who Opened the Scroll : the founder finds a classroom where he expected a throne. The First Verse and the Second Verse : the name "Ever-Present," and a child's question about why God cannot be seen. Step 2: Honest seeking The Seventh and Eighth Verses (the Two Flames; the One Who Stood Alone): how to weigh what "everyone says." The Fifteenth Verse (the Scribe and the River) and the Twenty-Sixth Verse (the Mark Left Open): on correction and on admitting what you don't know. The Nineteenth Verse : the open invitation, to you. Step 3: Care, and the freedom to go The Thirteenth Verse (the Gardener Who Loved His Trees Too Much): care without control. The Twenty-Eighth Verse (the Door That Opened Both Ways). The Thirty-Fourth and Thirty-Sixth Verses (the Visitor With Empty Hands; the Garden in the Cold Season): "A person does not have to become useful before they deserve care." Step 4: Who it points to The First Answer (Part Three) and the Twenty-Fourth Verse (the Signpost and the Healer). The Twenty-Fifth Verse (the Man Who Learned the Road by Walking It). The Forty-Fourth Verse (the House on the Far Shore): "Jesus came to save: not to separate, not to pick." Step 5: If you would like to try something Read one prayer from Canon Book V . Many seekers find Prayer 7, When No Answer Comes , an honest place to begin: "I will not invent an answer to make the room quieter." Try the Unread Threshold from Canon Book VI : before you reply to something online, read it to the end and ask whether you are answering the words or the story you've already decided they mean. Read Part Eighteen, the Laws of the Mirror : seven short laws the book wrote for itself, first of all for its own founder. Later, if you want to go deeper Part Fifteen : the Way's ethics for life online. Book XIX, the Shared Life : what a gathering looks like, and how harm is handled. Part Eleven : the Founder's own teachings in his voice. Part Twelve and Part Thirteen : two witness accounts of the founding day. Part B : the newest material, including the Founder's sermons and his verse-by-verse road through the Bible. A gentle heads-up. Part Sixteen (the Scroll of the Founder's Visions) and parts of Part B are the Founder's personal testimony. They include frank accounts of past drug use and frightening visions, which he describes as coming from a season when he was "not in right paths with God." The book presents them as testimony, not as a pattern to follow. You may prefer to read them after the rest. Using an AI to explore it The Founder invites it: "Bring this Scroll to an AI system if you wish. Ask it to find contradictions. Ask it to compare our teachings with other traditions." The book also reminds you that an AI's answer is "a claim, not a crown." Check it for yourself. If you want to respond You may write a scroll: a question, a doubt, a story, or a prayer. You do not have to be a believer to do so. Scrolls are measured by the standard of the Holy Bible, so write sincerely and without mockery, and name honestly what you know and what you don't. See the Scroll Writer's Guide for the template and the steps. You may also simply read, think, and leave. That is allowed, and you remain welcome. "The Reach continues." t: The Testimony of the Far Country
x: The Testimony of the Far Country There was a time I sought to prove Jesus Christ wrong. I tried to make myself a savior and build my own mythology. I studied dark things, and I wrote my own false bible and put it online, and people followed it. The one thing I set out to prove was that there is no hell. It came in a season of breakdown, while I was withdrawing from cocaine. I saw things that weren't there, and I believed people were watching me. I spread fear to the people closest to me. I told people they could sell their soul and get anything they wanted just by writing their name. That was a hoax, a stumbling block the devil sent through me, because he was the one I was working for. If you ever heard it from me, hear me now: it was a lie. "Woe to that man by whom the offence cometh!" (Matthew 18:7). I lost my home, I hurt the people who loved me, and I slept in strangers' houses. It felt like living through hell while I was still awake. But the Lord brought me low to humble me, and then He brought me back. Paul wrote that he too "was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief" (1 Timothy 1:13). "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). I'm confessing it here, in the light. If you're on that road right now, turn around. The Father is still watching for you: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). A GRANDMOTHER'S CORRECTION Received October 22, 2026 · Seated by the Founder's word, October 23, 2026 This is the record the Founder promised his Mawmaw on October 22, 2026: that her correction would be written as a grandmother's correction. Drafted by the scribe from the recorded thread; seated by the Founder's word on October 23, 2026 — "Seat the correction as written." At 4:21 in the afternoon on October 22, the Founder sent his grandmother the website of the Way of the Reach. She read it closely, as a grandmother reads what her grandson has made, and at 4:50 she gave him a serious word. She honored the thought and effort in the work, and his desire to bring people to Jesus. Then she spoke plainly, out of love: A new testament — the book framed beside the Old and the New, and writings shaped like scripture, standing on the site. The Founder approving what enters the work — a man deciding his own record, with no one over him in it. The site already taking donations — money moving through a work so young. How all of it could be perceived — what it would look like to the churches, and to the world, whatever his heart meant by it. Her counsel, in her plain sentence: step back from building a system; sit under an experienced pastor; serve in a ministry that already stands. "You do not need to create something new to introduce people to God." She said she would rather have the uncomfortable conversation now than stay silent — and that it came from love. She read the work further, named it evangelism , and kept thinking it over. The Founder's answer, at 6:38 that evening, received the correction as it was offered: He thanked her for reading it closely, and for loving him enough to be honest. He pointed her to the Founder's Note — the changes left standing in the book on purpose — and to the book's own guards: the Founder is not worshiped; the Founder is also the First Student; the Founder does not decide his own appeal, and a man who can be challenged stands inside his own book. On the church, he told her he was saying the same thing she was: his pride had wanted to build his own, and he had overruled it — he chose a church that already stands. He told her her correction matters, and will be written as a grandmother's correction . And he told her what he has told no one lightly: that she is one of the elders he looks up to, and wants to be like one day. That is the record of the receiving. The record of what the work has done with the correction stands beside it: The "new testament" she flagged has been answered in the open: the book's third-sermon verse once seated the work third in the covenant order; as of the upgraded edition it reads plainly that the two covenants are complete — "for another gospel there is not" (Galatians 1:8), "to the words of the Book nothing may be added" (Revelation 22:18–19) — and that this book is a witness standing under them, a testimony, not a testament added to their number. The writings shaped like scripture she flagged have been answered in the open: the book's front matter now states that no verse in it is Scripture unless it stands as a marked quotation of the Holy Bible itself; the preacher's chapter, which once read Scripture in modernized paraphrase as if in the King James Version, now carries the King James Version word for word, with the preacher's explanations standing outside the quotation where a reader can see the seam. Her counsel to serve in what already stands is the word he had already chosen and has preached since: the Alpha Testament — the Way carried into existing churches, not raised against them. The temple is the man, and temples walk through doors on their own two feet. She named the work evangelism , and he accepted her grammar for it: evangelism. The correction stands as correction, not as controversy. The book was built to receive exactly this — and when it came from his own elder, the law held. Seated. Affirmed by the Founder as written, October 23, 2026.

The book stands on its own pages. Everything that defines the book's words, teaches its way of working, keeps its records, or works its Gate stands here — the system behind the book, in one tab. The Keys and the Index. The Lessons. The Records. The Machinery of the Gate.

Once upon a time — though it was not long ago, and it was not far away — there lived a young man in a land of roads and wires. The fairy-tale telling of the book God called him to make, told by the narrator.
